o: Two numbers are almost equal if ≤2 digit swaps transform one into the other (leading zeros allowed). Pad each number to its natural digit string; generate its full reachable set: identity, all single transpositions (≤ C(7,2)=21), and all compositions of two transpositions (≤ ~441). Two numbers are almost equal iff their reachable sets intersect. Count pairs by streaming numbers through variant buckets, crediting each pair once when its later member arrives (dedupe equal values first, since identical numbers are trivially almost equal).
k: Swaps act on positions, so the reachable set = {identity} ∪ {transpositions} ∪ {products of two transpositions} applied to the digit string — at most a few hundred variants per number.
Count pairs once by processing numbers in order: for each new number, collect the set of earlier indices sharing any variant, then register its variants.

a.n: Approach 1: Variant generation with bucket-based pair counting
a.i: For each distinct value, enumerate ≤2-swap variants as integers (leading zeros collapse naturally). Maintain variant → earlier indices. When processing x, the number of valid pairs (earlier, x) equals the size of the union of earlier-index lists over x's variants; adding that union size counts each pair exactly once.
s: Dedupe equal values; add C(c,2) for each multiplicity c.
For each distinct value (in insertion order), generate its variant set (string swaps, parse back to int).
Look up each variant's bucket to gather earlier indices into a hash set; add its size to the answer.
Append the current index to every variant bucket.
a.t: O(D·V²) generation plus bucket scans — D ≤ 5000 distinct values, V ≈ 462 variants; worst-case bucket scans degrade with heavy collisions but pass in practice

a.n: Approach 2: Signature canonicalization for the Easy-version style
a.i: For the 1-swap version, sorting the digit multiset gives a canonical signature; groups of equal signatures contribute C(c,2) pairs. This fails for 2 swaps (not all permutations are reachable), but is a useful warm-up and sanity check for the machinery.
s: Pad each number to a string; signature = sorted digits.
Cross-check small cases against Approach 1 to understand why 2 swaps breaks it.
a.t: O(n·L log L) — sorting each short digit string

w: Approach 1 is the correct general solution; the signature method only works for the 1-swap variant (worth mentioning in an interview to show understanding of why transposition closure matters). Pitfalls: leading zeros after swaps (parse via int/stoi handles it), double-counting pairs sharing multiple variants (fixed by the seen-set union), and overflow (use 64-bit for pair counts). Follow-up: allow at most k swaps — reachable sets grow combinatorially; meet-in-the-middle or BFS over digit-string states with depth ≤ k becomes necessary.
